agritech-f9202a9e43.headline: GSK Signs 8-Year Carbon Removal Deal With Varaha to Scale Regenerative Farming in India
agritech-f9202a9e43.fulltext:
Global healthcare company GSK has signed an eight-year deal with Indian climate company Varaha to cut emissions and enhance carbon removal. It will support regenerative agriculture on 50,000 hectares of smallholder farmland in Punjab and Haryana.
The deal was structured by climate investment platform Earthly and covers more than 500,000 carbon credits. The project is expected to deliver about 100,000 tonnes of removal credits a year between 2028 and 2033. The wider agreement runs for eight years.
The project will help farmers move away from crop residue burning, intensive tillage and flood-irrigated rice farming. Instead, farmers will use practices such as direct-seeded rice, reduced tillage and crop-residue incorporation.
The deal is notable because it links carbon finance with three major issues in northern India: climate change, farm income and air pollution.
Adele Cheli, VP Environmental Sustainability at GSK, said:
“For GSK, environmental sustainability is core to business resilience and human health. This investment demonstrates how we’re progressing in our net-zero journey, whilst also delivering co-benefits for human health, nature and local communities.”
Carbon Finance Targets India’s Crop Burning Problem
Farmers in Punjab and Haryana often burn rice residue after harvest because they have only a short period to prepare fields for the next crop. India has been working to reduce the practice, and the number of farm fires has fallen sharply.
During the 2025 paddy season, Punjab recorded 5,114 farm-fire incidents, down 53% from 2024. Haryana recorded 662, also a 53% fall. Together, the two states recorded about a 90% reduction from 2022 levels.
Despite that progress, the government continues to identify crop-residue burning as an important source of seasonal air pollution in northern India.
The carbon project aims to address the economic reasons farmers burn the residue. Farmers will receive subsidized access to machinery and a share of carbon credit revenue.
That can help cover the extra cost and labour needed to manage crop residues without burning them. This makes the carbon market part of the solution rather than simply paying for an emissions calculation after the fact.
Regenerative Farming Targets Carbon, Water and Farm Income
The Varaha project is designed to generate both emissions reductions and soil carbon removals.
Reduced tillage can lower fuel use and soil disturbance. Direct-seeded rice can reduce the need for intensive field preparation and flooding. Incorporating crop residues into the soil can also return organic matter to farmland.
Varaha’s project has already reported results from an earlier monitoring period covering 42,000 hectares. The project estimated it avoided about 4,574 tonnes of PM2.5 emissions from crop burning. It also saved around 59.5 billion litres of water.
Moreover, participating households saw an average 12% to 16% increase in income. This rise came from higher yields, lower fertilizer costs, and carbon revenue.
The water figure is particularly notable. Across the 42,000-hectare monitoring area, the reported savings work out to roughly 1.4 million litres per hectare.
These figures are project results, not a guarantee for the full 50,000-hectare expansion. Future performance will depend on farmer adoption, weather, crop yields and verification.
The Project Uses Verra’s Agricultural Carbon Methodology
The project is registered under the Verra Verified Carbon Standard, using VM0042 Improved Agricultural Land Management. Earthly says it is also upgrading the project to version 2.2 of the methodology. The project is listed on the Verra system as Project 3346.
VM0042 covers greenhouse gas reductions and soil organic carbon removals from improved farming practices. These include reduced tillage, better fertilizer use, and residue and water management.
The updated VM0042 v2.2 is approved by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market as meeting its Core Carbon Principles (CCP) requirements. However, that does not automatically give every project or credit a CCP label. Projects must meet additional conditions at verification.
Those rules are important for agricultural carbon because soil carbon can be difficult to measure and can change over time. The updated methodology includes stronger requirements around baselines, additionality, leakage, and soil carbon measurement.
GSK Is Building a Larger Carbon Removal Portfolio
The Varaha deal fits directly into GSK’s broader climate strategy. The pharma giant plans to reduce 80% of greenhouse gas emissions from all scopes by 2030, using a 2020 baseline. Nature-based solutions will address the final 20%.
It also targets net zero across its full value chain by 2045, including a 90% absolute emissions reduction and neutralization of residual emissions. GSK says it prioritizes carbon removals for its 2030 target and plans to use only carbon removals for its 2045 net-zero target.
The company announced that by the end of 2025, it had secured carbon credits for 8% of its expected residual emissions. This is 40% of the credits it anticipates needing.
The Varaha agreement, therefore, adds to a growing pipeline of nature-based carbon projects that GSK is developing ahead of its future residual emissions needs. Importantly, GSK says carbon credits are being used alongside direct emissions cuts, rather than as a replacement for them.
Agriculture Is Becoming a Larger Carbon Market
The deal also shows why agriculture is becoming an important part of the carbon removal market. Verra said in 2025 that around 200 projects were listed under earlier versions of VM0042. Together, those projects had the potential to issue an estimated 126 million tonnes of emissions reductions and removals annually.
That is potential supply, not actual issuance. Still, it shows the size of the pipeline being developed around improved farming practices.
Agricultural projects can also offer benefits that are difficult to obtain from some industrial carbon removal technologies. These include improved soil health, lower water use, better farm resilience, and additional income for farmers.
At the same time, they face measurement challenges. Soil carbon changes slowly and can vary between fields. Weather and farming practices can also affect results. That makes strong measurement and independent verification essential for buyers such as GSK.
A Long-Term Deal Gives Farmers More Certainty
One of the most important parts of the agreement is its length. Many voluntary carbon transactions are relatively short-term purchases. An eight-year commitment helps Varaha see future demand better. This can support investments in farm equipment, field support, and measurement systems.
That matters because farmers need to change practices before carbon benefits can be measured.
The project also includes ongoing reporting. Earthly says the agreement includes quarterly reporting covering carbon, water, farmer income, and community engagement through the project period. This wider reporting is becoming more important as buyers look beyond the number of tonnes generated.
The Deal Is a Test for High-Quality Farm Carbon
The GSK-Varaha agreement is significant because it moves beyond a small demonstration project. The planned 50,000 hectares represent a large expansion of regenerative farming in a region where crop burning, water use, and soil management remain major challenges.
However, the more important test will be delivery. The project must show that farmers maintain the new practices, that soil carbon gains are measured accurately, and that the claimed emissions reductions are independently verified.
For GSK, the deal adds a significant source of future removals as it works toward its 2030 and 2045 climate targets. For Varaha, it provides long-term demand to scale regenerative agriculture. And for India’s farmers, the model could create another source of income while reducing burning and improving soil management.
For the carbon market, long-term corporate commitments can help turn agricultural carbon projects into real investments in climate, farming, and public health.

agritech-c73a9318c0.headline: 10 days left: Monsoon almost over, India's rain deficit at 15%, recovery bleak
agritech-c73a9318c0.fulltext:
10 days left: Monsoon almost over, India's rain deficit at 15%, recovery bleak
India's southwest monsoon is entering its final phase with a 15 per cent rainfall deficit still in place. With withdrawal set to begin over parts of northwest India, the window for any meaningful recovery is narrowing.
India’s 2026 southwest monsoon has entered its final stretch with the country’s rainfall deficit still standing at 15 per cent, leaving little time for the monsoon to make up the shortfall before its withdrawal.
According to the latest India Meteorological Department (IMD) rainfall data for June 1 to September 20, India has received 699.7 mm of rainfall against the normal 822 mm, resulting in a 15 per cent deficit.
With the monsoon expected to begin withdrawing from large parts of northwest India over the next five to seven days, the window for a significant recovery is narrowing rapidly.
For Delhi-NCR, the 2026 monsoon is effectively nearing its end, with weather models suggesting limited prospects of meaningful rainfall for the remainder of September.
This leaves little scope for the national rainfall deficit to improve substantially from the region.
The situation, however, could be different over parts of north India.
Weather models indicate that Uttar Pradesh and Bihar could see their most significant spell of September rainfall between September 25 and 28. Such rainfall could provide some late-season relief to the two states, although its impact on the overall national deficit will depend on the intensity and geographical spread of the rains.
The latest IMD map shows large variations in rainfall across the country. Several central and eastern states have recorded rainfall close to normal, while parts of northwest and southern India remain in the deficient category.
Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala are among the regions showing rainfall deficits in the latest assessment.
In contrast, several parts of central and eastern India have remained within the normal rainfall range.
The monsoon's withdrawal is now becoming the bigger factor.
Once the southwest monsoon retreats from a region, the possibility of widespread monsoon rainfall reduces sharply. Any late-season rainfall would therefore depend largely on individual weather systems, including low-pressure areas, disturbances and changes in atmospheric circulation.
The latest satellite imagery also shows widespread cloud activity over parts of central, eastern and southern India, but this does not necessarily translate into sustained rainfall across the country.
For India as a whole, the next 10 days could therefore be crucial. A few strong rainfall spells could reduce the deficit, but the approaching withdrawal means there is increasingly little time for the monsoon to erase the shortfall.
The 2026 monsoon, which began with a significant rainfall deficit during its early phase before recovering in July and August, is now heading towards its final phase with the country still 15 per cent below its long-period average.

indian-startups-18baec66e6.headline: India’s Spacetech Gold Rush Is Here, But What’s Making Investors Jittery?
indian-startups-18baec66e6.fulltext: The Indian spacetech ecosystem is entering its most critical phase yet. After years of experimentation and ambition, spacetech startups must now prove they are on a path to commercial viability. Investors are already betting on this transition. According to Inc42's data, homegrown spacetech startups have already raised $252.9 Mn so far this year, nearly double what the sector raised in 2025. Leading the momentum is Skyroot Aerospace. The startup became India’s first spacetech unicorn in May after it raised a $60 Mn round. Subsequently, it was successful in becoming the first Indian private company to place a rocket into orbit with its Vikram-1 mission. It is now lining up a bigger $200 Mn round. Earlier this month, Temasek-backed hyperspectral imaging startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C round made headlines as the single-largest funding round raised by a spacetech startup in India. So, why are spacetech startups suddenly the flavour of the season? A key reason is the deepening policy push. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) earlier this year began deploying capital from its ₹1,600 Cr Antariksh Venture Capital Fund. Similarly, the state-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) fund also recently allocated nearly ₹834 Cr to spacetech startups in its inaugural cohort. The buzz around the sector hasn’t just been about money coming in, but real achievements too. GalaxEye recently became the first Indian startup to secure a US patent for its OptoSAR satellite imaging technology. Agnikul Cosmos also completed a test firing of its Agnite engine, which boasts India’s first semi-cryogenic engine and the largest 3D-printed single-piece rocket engine in the world. Despite this, finding commercial viability is a looming concern for many spacetech startups. In addition, there are concerns around the frothy spacetech valuations. Under the current scheme of things, can Indian spacetech startups convert milestones into scalable and sustainable business models? What Are VCs Betting On? Earlier this year, Union minister of state (MoS) Jitendra Singh pegged the size of India’s space economy at around $9 Bn and projected that it would grow to nearly $45 Bn over the next decade. Behind this projected market size is an entire value chain: First comes the infrastructure layer that enables launches, including ground stations, launch vehicles, and the components that act as inputs for the rockets Then come payloads – the satellites and sensors that hitch a ride on the rocket and generate data from orbit From there comes the ‘downstream’ data intelligence and applications layer, comprising analytics and services that process the raw data from the previous step. It is this ‘downstream’ layer that Viju George, a partner at Mela Ventures, believes has the most promise. “Revenue models in satellites tend to be very lumpy and capex-driven, whereas data streams tend to be high-margin recurring revenue,” he observed. The upstream input layer is relatively more commoditised, as per George. But that doesn’t mean it’s not investable. “If you’re able to take the shovels approach, where you provide the components to satellites like avionics, communication infrastructure, and others, that is a kind of a multipurpose play. With that positioning, you're not really dependent on a single satellite brand winning or losing,” he added. Ashish Taneja of GrowX Ventures, an early investor in Pixxel, also believes that the nascent earth observation segment is a huge market opportunity. He added that the infrastructure layer is a “big thing too” as it continues to be a supply-constrained market. But have the potential and the promise of spacetech taken investors too far? The Gap Between Hype & Market Demand The rapid influx of capital into the spacetech sector is creating concerns around valuations, market size and whether the demand required to justify these bets has materialised yet. “I worry about the valuations because now somehow we are in the FOMO zone,” George said, adding that he is unsure whether the market is large enough to support current valuations. The risk, he said, is “whether you are paying a little bit more for market demand that is not yet evident.” The valuation question is especially pronounced for capex-heavy businesses, where large cheques are being signed based on potential future launch cadence and scale, even as India’s launch capacity is still developing. Space hardware also carries risks around technology, manufacturing, launch and satellite longevity. Satellites are expected to operate for around five to six years, but India does not yet have enough historical data to establish how reliably newer constellations will perform over that period. Because of limited launch experience and deployments, investors are finding it tough to benchmark execution capability or predictable revenues. The growing number of startups is also raising the investment bar, with multiple ventures now attacking similar problems. To achieve scale, spacetech startups will need to expand their base beyond government buying, which has, thus far, acted as an anchor customer. These emerging players will also need to tap into foreign sovereign buyers and commercial enterprises as well. But demonstrating competitive cost, reliability, performance and consistency will be key to competing in international markets. As such, GrowX’s Taneja remarks that “not many people will make the cut” in attracting sustained capital, predicting consolidation as startups expand beyond their initial products and become vertically integrated space infrastructure companies. Simply put, he believes that stronger players could eventually acquire or absorb smaller companies. What Will It Take To Win Capital? The first phase of Indian spacetech hinged on visions and ideas. But growing market maturity and an influx of new ventures have turned investor focus to identifying which businesses can turn technical breakthroughs into large, durable markets. A startup may solve an extremely difficult engineering or deeptech problem, but that alone does not guarantee a scalable business. “Early stage investors like to see milestones because we think they are the precursor to valuations and revenues. But once growth investors come in, they like to see tangible metrics,” said Mela Ventures’ George. In 2018-19, investors were largely evaluating founder quality, technical capabilities, and whether building satellites and propulsion systems out of India was even possible. This is no longer the case. “I want a precise use case. I want clarity on the use case. I want a differentiated solution which is defensible in the long run,” said Taneja. Investors also want clarity on who will buy the product, how it will be used and what makes the offering difficult to replicate. Hence, established spacetech startups have more of an advantage now in attracting growth funding as they have a track record to show. Signs of market maturity are also evident with global investors now participating in larger rounds, while domestic growth-stage funds are also beginning to enter Series B and beyond. But the funding pool remains smaller, particularly for capital-intensive spacetech businesses that require significant funding before reaching scale. This could make the public markets increasingly relevant to the sector's long-term funding cycle. Once companies have spent years building technology, establishing revenues and reaching sufficient scale, public listings could provide another route to capital and liquidity. For early investors, meanwhile, the long development cycle itself can create multiple opportunities for valuation repricing as spacetech startups move from technical milestones to commercial deployment. Taneja cited a 17X outcome over around five years, following the sale of a small portion of GrowX’s stake during Pixxel’s recent $100 Mn fundraise. Regardless, the investment thesis has evolved substantially from when the first spacetech startups created the market a decade ago. The real challenge now is not reaching the stars, but turning that journey into a stellar business.

indian-startups-dcca8c1fe6.headline: Drivn Raises Rs 45 Crore From Avaana Capital, Seed Shares Priced at Rs 132.40 Apiece
indian-startups-dcca8c1fe6.fulltext:
Gurugram-based electric mobility startup Drivn has secured Rs 45 crore in seed funding for its Indian business, adding fresh equity capital months after lining up financing commitments of up to $80 million with Nomura for electric buses and trucks.
Electric mobility startup Drivn has raised Rs 45 crore, or about $4.7 million, in seed funding from Avaana Capital through its Indian entity. The investment brings institutional capital into a business that is building an electric mobility platform around commercial vehicles rather than focusing only on vehicle ownership.
It is in the finer points of the transaction where the contours of the deal become clearer. The Indian arm of Drivn had approved the issuance of 33,98,792 compulsorily convertible preference shares at the price of Rs 132.40 per share to Avaana Capital, who have invested the entire amount of Rs 45 crore in this regard.
The share price and post-round ownership structure make this more than a headline funding announcement. Following the investment, Avaana Capital holds a 7.22% stake in Drivn’s Indian entity, while Singapore-based Drivn Transition PTE. LTD retains 88.75%. Co-founder Manav Bansal holds the remaining 4.03%, based on the filings cited in the report.
Drivn is building around commercial electric fleets
Founded in 2025 by Manav Bansal, Alpna Jain and Madhujeet Chimni, Drivn Transition Private Limited is based in Gurugram and is focused on electrifying commercial vehicle operations.
Its model goes beyond supplying electric vehicles. The company is developing a platform that brings together vehicle leasing, charging, battery lifecycle management and fleet operations for commercial EV users.
Drivn owns and leases electric commercial vehicles, including intercity buses and heavy-duty trucks. The broader proposition is built around tackling some of the practical requirements involved in fleet electrification, including financing, deployment and supporting infrastructure.
On the financing side, its offering includes long-tenure leases, flexible payment structures and operating lease models. Drivn also uses a technology platform to track vehicle and battery performance, bringing the operating and financial sides of commercial EV deployment into the same business model.
Rs 45 crore equity round follows Nomura financing commitment
The Avaana Capital investment comes after Drivn secured a separate financing commitment of up to $80 million from Japanese financial group Nomura.
The combination gives Drivn two distinct pools of capital as it develops its commercial EV platform. The equity round strengthens the company at the corporate level, while the earlier financing commitment was directed toward putting electric commercial vehicles on the road.
The Singapore entity has also invested in the Indian operation previously, with foreign investment data listing Drivn Transition PTE. LTD as an investor in Drivn Transition Private Limited.
For Drivn, the latest round therefore sits within a wider capital strategy built around both ownership funding and deployment financing. With Avaana now holding 7.22% of the Indian business and the Singapore entity remaining the controlling shareholder, the company enters its next phase with fresh seed capital alongside the previously announced financing capacity for buses and heavy-duty trucks.

Vaamanaa Sethi
Updated20 Sep 2026, 11:17 AM IST
Brokerage firm Jefferies in a report said that large domestic opportunity is driving private participation in emergent industries in India across Space, Semi & Electronics, Datacenters and Solar.
The brokerage firm further said that support from the government is also visible here with action such as opening up space to private sector, long tax holiday for DCs, large incentive schemes for Semi, Electronics & Solar, localisation requirements, GPU purchases etc.
Private sector takes India’s space industry to the next level. India is one of the few countries with strong and globally competitive space capabilities.
The government opened the space sector to private companies in 2020 and aims to grow the space economy nearly fivefold between 2023 and 2030 to $40–45 billion.
Startups are now moving from early-stage innovation to commercial operations, with companies such as Skyroot working on orbital launches, Pixxel developing high-resolution Earth-observation satellites, Agnikul building 3D-printed rocket engines, and Digantara developing satellites for space surveillance, said the firm.
According to the report, India’s semiconductor ambitions are moving from plans to actual execution, with around $20 billion in investments. This includes a chip fabrication plant under construction and several OSAT projects that are starting production.
A new $13 billion incentive plan is expected to further strengthen the ecosystem and increase value addition, including in chip design. While challenges such as supply-chain development, skilled talent and global competition remain, India is laying the foundation for a strong semiconductor industry.
India’s data centre sector is quickly becoming a key part of the country’s digital infrastructure. Colocation capacity has grown five times in the last five years to around 2 GW, driven by increasing cloud adoption, digitalisation and data localisation requirements.
“We expect capacity to grow another 5x to ~10GW over the next five years, supported by favorable cost economics, policy support and rising hyperscaler demand. We calculate this expansion represents a US$9bn revenue opportunity for data center operators and a US$45bn investment opportunity across power, cooling, construction and network infrastructure,” the report said.
India’s electronics industry is moving beyond assembly towards greater domestic value addition and component manufacturing. Electronics exports have grown significantly, while initiatives such as ECMS and MPMS (Mobile 2.0) are aimed at strengthening local component production, increasing backward integration and reducing dependence on imports.
“We forecast ECMS to cover ~50% of Mobile component value (BoM) over the next 6-Y vs <20% now. PCB (both HDI + Multi-layer) is a focus area for Components, with S5bn TAM, 85-90% imports,” the report added.
India has become the world’s second-largest solar PV manufacturer, with around 35 GW of solar cell manufacturing capacity already operational and another 100 GW under construction. Government measures such as ALMM (Approved List of Models and Manufacturers), domestic content requirements and PLI (Production-Linked Incentive) schemes are helping expand local manufacturing of solar cells, wafers and ingots. The firm anticipates that by 2030, around 90% of the solar manufacturing value chain is expected to be localised in India.
For Aerospace sector, the report said that India is emerging as a key beneficiary of the growing global demand for aerospace products. The country has an opportunity to benefit from its cost-competitive manufacturing capabilities and skilled engineering talent.
Indian aerospace exports are also growing, with Boeing and Airbus already sourcing products worth around $1.4–1.6 billion annually from India. Companies such as Aequs, Azad, BHFC, DYTC, Rane, Motherson and Sansera have become suppliers to global aircraft manufacturers and Tier-1 companies and are steadily expanding their presence in the aerospace sector.

india-03316c4365.headline: 'Historic occasion': Jaishankar describes first V4+India Foreign Ministers meeting
india-03316c4365.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-03316c4365.fulltext:
India and the four-member Visegrad group of Central European countries on Monday (September 21, 2026) agreed to step up political, economic and defence cooperation at their first Foreign Ministers' meeting, which External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar described as a “new historic occasion”.
The Visegrad Group (V4) is a cultural and political alliance of the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia that aims to advance cooperation in military, economic, cultural, and energy affairs.
The first meeting between the Foreign Ministers of the Visegrad Group and India was held on Monday (September 21, 2026), on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
Mr Jaishankar met with Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Radek Sikorski; Hungary's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Anita Orban; Slovakia's Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Juraj Blanar; and the Czech Minister of Foreign Affairs, Petr Macinka.
"It was, in a sense, a new historic occasion,” Mr. Jaishankar said in remarks after the meeting.
"It was a very, very productive meeting. What we agreed was that since India's relationship with the European Union itself is deepening, with the V4 we would take some special initiatives to create an annual business forum,” he said, adding that there was “consensus" that the Foreign Ministers of the five nations in the group would meet annually.
“We would also explore technology and innovation whether we could be doing more. We have a very strong history with all the V4 countries in defence. We want to refresh and take forward that record and that cooperation,” Mr. Jaishankar said.
The group also discussed issues including space, connectivity, and people-to-people mobility.
Mr. Jaishankar said the meeting was “very worthwhile” and “very productive”, with discussions focusing on cooperation as well as major global crises, including the Ukraine conflict and developments in the Gulf.
“It was really a very, very worthwhile, very productive meeting. I'm very pleased about it,” he said in remarks to reporters after the meeting.
In a post on X, Mr. Jaishankar said the first meeting in the V4+India format agreed to closer political cooperation, including annual meetings of foreign ministers, and deeper economic cooperation, including the Annual Business Forum.
The countries also agreed to strengthen technology, innovation, research and education partnerships; reinvigorate defence cooperation; further develop cultural cooperation and people-to-people relations and work together to support multilateralism, he said.
Mr. Jaishankar also said that India has “very good” relations with the V4 countries.
"These are countries with a very strong, very distinctive capability. These are industrial economies, economies with great innovation and technology talent, and I think how the V4 come together is for them to decide. But we certainly welcome the opportunity to work with the V4 together,” he told reporters.

india-af94de21e1.headline: 100% drought likely to be declared in Maharashtra by month-end, says Minister
india-af94de21e1.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-af94de21e1.fulltext:
Maharashtra Cooperation Minister Babasaheb Patil on Monday said the BJP-led Mahayuti government will soon declare 100% drought in the State. Speaking on the severity of the crisis, Mr. Patil said, “In my entire life, I have never seen such a severe drought. All crops, including soya bean, cotton and sugarcane, have suffered due to the dry spell and the loss is huge. The 100% drought declaration is expected by the end of September based on the National Disaster Response Fund norms.”
The Minister said the government has already initiated measures such as fee waiver for students, electricity bill waiver, and deployment of water tankers to provide relief.
The statement assumes significance as it is the first time a Minister has spoken of a 100% drought declaration. So far, the official position of the government has been that crop damage surveys and ground verification would be conducted after October 5.
Several regions in the State have been facing a prolonged dry spell, causing extensive crop loss and forcing farmers to incur heavy losses. According to the State Agriculture Department, rainfall has remained absent for over 20 days in at least 83 talukas across 20 districts. At least six districts, including Amravati, Solapur and Latur, have recorded rainfall deficit of 40-50%. Water tankers have started plying in villages such as Naichakur in Dharashiv district.
Advisory to districts
In view of the crisis, the State government has instructed district administrations to revive existing water sources and build water supply networks in villages facing shortage instead of treating tankers as the first solution.
A circular issued by the State Soil and Water Conservation Department on September 16 stated that the Groundwater Surveys and Development Agency will identify villages with drinking water shortage and submit the list to District Collectorates by October. District Collectors will have to plan interventions for the villages for the period between October and December. The plans are to be submitted by November 15, followed by plans for January-March 2027 by December 20, and for April-June 2027 by January 20, it stated.
Meanwhile, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Monday said the government would not wait for Central assistance to help farmers facing distress due to inadequate rainfall. “A formal crop loss assessment would be carried out after October 5 as required under the rules, following which the State would seek assistance from the Centre,” he told reporters.

world-ea16baaac9.fulltext:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico file lawsuit against Trump's White House ban
- Published
CNN, Politico and MS NOW have said they will sue the Trump administration after the three US media outlets were barred from the White House.
President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".
Major US TV networks later suspended their White House pooled coverage of Trump as he headed to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
Trump, reacting to news of the lawsuit, called the news organisations "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements.
"Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that "almost without question" his team will file an appeal.
The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.
The statement from CNN, Politico and MS NOW said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
The media organisations filed the lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington, asking a judge to quickly rule Trump's ban unconstitutional and prevent his aides from enforcing it.
On Monday morning, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties, which sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.
Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.
The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place".
CNN - one of only five US news outlets in the White House press pool for live television - was originally due to cover Trump's trip to the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday and Tuesday.
But on Monday morning, the five-seat CNN booth in the basement of the White House press area - typically manned throughout the day from the early hours of the morning - was empty and closed. Screens and monitors inside were turned off.
Instead, a CNN crew was outside the secured area of the White House grounds, broadcasting live from a public pavement.
Five TV networks, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC, issued a joint statement: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.
"No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."
Those five networks are considered the only ones with the money and infrastructure to distribute live coverage from the White House and presidential events.
For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.
Several US outlets also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday.
Later on Monday, Trump met with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani for an hour-long discussion. Afterwards, the two held a news conference, which was covered by New York media.
"I told the president that we're going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn, and that is something that I believe in," Mamdani said.
Trump continued his criticism of the media at the event, saying that journalists always say that they will boycott, but they "never boycott" him.
On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel on its site called Trump TV, which began by replaying remarks from Trump during a visit to Mount Rushmore in July.
Announcing his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW last week, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".
The US president added that there "may be others to join them".
When later asked by a reporter what he meant by this, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.
The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS Now and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.
Trump has been frequently critical of news organisations and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

World leaders meet at UN as planet grapples with climate change, wars, runaway AI
As we face ‘three existential threats,’ says the UN chief, ‘international cooperation is more necessary than ever’
Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations in New York this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people.
The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: can the leaders do anything to end them?
And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth?
The future of the UN will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players.

other-interests-fd5d735f1a.fulltext:
For most objects, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. But if you are swimming upstream in a river of quantum light, the normal rules don’t apply. Physicists have demonstrated that breaking Isaac Newton’s third law of motion in such a setting can be useful, leading to new ways of controlling quantum light in experiments and devices.
Moving upstream against the current is possible, as some animals and boats do, but at the cost of expending energy. Yi Hu at Nankai University in China and his colleagues wondered whether a passive swimmer that doesn’t do so could still move upstream.
The researchers studied upstream swimming in a quantum system. Because past experiments established precise ways of controlling quantum light, they used it to make both their river and swimmer. They created this quantum light fluid by shooting lasers into a special crystal that was exposed to an electric voltage, which made the photons interact and form a river-like system. The swimmer was another beam of quantum light, but this one was shaped to form a single, solitary wave.
Advertisement
The action-reaction principle of Newton’s third law would have the swimmer and the river experience the same type of force – either repulsive or attractive – similar to how gravity leads to mutual attraction between our bodies and Earth. Earth attracts us downwards, and experiences an upwards attraction towards us. In contrast, in the experiment, the swimmer experienced an attractive interaction with the river, but the river experienced a repulsive force on the swimmer. This was a “non-reciprocal” interaction that breaks the action-reaction principle. Its net effect was an upstream force on the swimmer, says Hu.
“For me, the biggest takeaway is that active behaviour does not necessarily require an intrinsically active particle or swimmer,” he says.
Mathias Albert at Côte d’Azur University in France says that upstream motion has previously been achieved in other quantum fluids of light, but it always relied on creating tiny vortices behind the swimmer in the fluid, with the recoil from their creation pushing the swimmer, so the new experiment demonstrates a fundamentally different mechanism for motion.
We already know that non-reciprocal interactions can be crucial for shaping the motion of “active matter” systems where objects consume energy to move, such as bacterial mixtures, flocks of birds or swarms of tiny robots. But the experiments by Hu and his colleagues focused on an object that doesn’t consume energy, yet still benefited from non-reciprocal interactions. Their work could therefore usher in the creation of a new type of active matter in a quantum system.
“This question is very much in the air at the moment, with several groups exploring how the concepts of active matter can be combined with quantum fluids and photonic systems,” says Albert.
He says that, eventually, the ability to control chunks of light so they move in some preferred direction could be useful within devices that use quantum light. Such devices are prevalent in, for example, communications or quantum information processing.
Hu says that the team now wants to construct more complex experiments where they could control the swimmer’s motion more precisely or add several swimmers to the fluid at once.

other-interests-d4b61e4446.headline: These dolphins are shouting
other-interests-d4b61e4446.fulltext:
Pilot whales now need to shout to be heard over the rumble of ship traffic in the Strait of Gibraltar, the narrow strip of water between Morocco and Spain.
Researchers looked at near and long-distance communication between long-finned pilot whales (Globicephala melas), which are actually a species of large dolphin. They found the mammals were able to increase the volume of their calls used for short distances, but long-distance calling was more challenging, according to their recently published study.
The dolphins may not be able to overpower noise pollution in the Strait of Gibraltar when calling pod mates far away, raising concerns that they could become lost and isolated from the group, the researchers said. Roughly 60,000 ships pass through the Strait of Gibraltar each year.

Call for Applications: Tech Policy Press Fellowship 2027 – Apply By 24 September 2026
Tech Policy Press is inviting applications for its 2027 Fellowship Program, a year-long, part-time opportunity for mid-career journalists, researchers, lawyers and public policy professionals working on issues at the intersection of technology and democracy.
The fellowship is designed to support independent reporting and analysis on urgent technology-policy questions, including artificial intelligence governance, technology regulation, digital rights, democracy and the relationship between state and corporate power.
Applications are open to candidates worldwide, with particular encouragement for applicants from the Global Majority and communities that remain underrepresented in media and global technology-policy discussions.
The application deadline is September 24, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT.
Fellowship Benefits
Each selected fellow will receive a $10,000 stipend, distributed quarterly, to support their fellowship work. The program is part-time and conducted remotely, with fellows working as independent contractors.
In addition to financial support, participants will become part of an international cohort of fellows and receive ongoing editorial guidance from Tech Policy Press. Fellows will participate in monthly sessions focused on developing their work, exchanging ideas and receiving feedback.
The fellowship provides an opportunity to develop a substantial body of public-interest work over 12 months. Fellows can also build professional networks, develop relationships with sources in their areas of expertise and engage with an international community of journalists, researchers and policy professionals.
Tech Policy Press publishes fellows’ work on its website and promotes selected projects through its newsletter, podcast and special events, providing opportunities for their research and reporting to reach wider audiences.
Who Can Apply?
The fellowship is intended for mid-career professionals with demonstrated experience or expertise in technology policy, media, public policy or related fields.
Applicants may have expertise in a particular technology-policy issue, geographic region or broader questions concerning technology’s effects on democracy and society. International applicants are eligible, including candidates who are not authorised to work in the United States.
The program particularly welcomes applications from the Global Majority and underrepresented communities in media. There is no specific preferred geographic or thematic focus for applicants from the Global South.
Candidates should be able to demonstrate strong writing and analytical abilities and propose an area of focus that explains what they intend to explore and why their background makes them well suited to the topic.
Fellowship Responsibilities
Fellows are expected to produce analysis or reporting related to technology and democracy at least monthly throughout the fellowship. While the subject matter can evolve during the year, applicants should begin with a clearly defined area of interest.
Participants must also attend a mandatory monthly cohort meeting and a monthly check-in with the Tech Policy Press editorial team. Fellows are expected to collaborate with other fellows and the organisation’s editorial team where appropriate, meet agreed deadlines and disclose potential conflicts of interest.
The fellowship commences in January 2027 and continues for 12 months.
Application Requirements
Applicants must complete the online application form by September 24, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT.
The application requires:
- A CV or resume
- A cover letter of no more than two pages explaining what the applicant hopes to accomplish
- Links to previous published work
- Two professional references
Writing samples should generally have been published within the previous three years and must be publicly accessible. Acceptable examples may include reported articles, policy analyses, essays, opinion pieces, podcasts, newsletters or data projects.
At least one submitted piece must have been originally written in English. Unpublished research papers, dissertations and class assignments are not accepted as published work.
How to Strengthen an Application
Applicants can strengthen their submissions by clearly defining a technology-policy issue, explaining its public-interest significance and demonstrating relevant experience through strong published work.
The proposed focus should show how the applicant intends to contribute original reporting or analysis. Applicants from regions and communities that are often overlooked in global technology-policy debates can use their contextual knowledge and professional experience to explain perspectives that may be underrepresented.
Professional references should come from individuals who can credibly speak to the applicant’s writing quality or ability to produce public-interest work related to technology and democracy.
Application Deadline and Selection
Applications close on September 24, 2026. Tech Policy Press expects to notify applicants about their status by early December 2026. A shortlisted group may be invited to participate in one online interview.
The fellowship follows a highly competitive application process. Tech Policy Press reported receiving more than 2,000 applications for approximately 8–10 fellowship places in the previous application cycle.
Information Sessions and Application Route
Tech Policy Press is offering information sessions for prospective applicants through Zoom. Interested candidates should register through the organisation’s official fellowship announcement for available session details.
Applications should be submitted through the official online application form before the stated deadline. Prospective applicants with additional questions can contact [email protected].
Official Opportunity
The Tech Policy Press Fellowship 2027 offers a structured platform for experienced professionals to produce independent work examining technology’s relationship with democracy and society. With a $10,000 stipend, editorial support, international peer exchange and opportunities to publish work, the program is intended to support sustained public-interest reporting and analysis.
International candidates, including professionals based outside the United States, are eligible to apply.

Call For Applications: Citizen AI Arts & Technology Fellowship 2026-2027 | $3,000 Stipend
Applications are open for the Citizen AI Arts & Technology Fellowship 2026–2027, a fellowship bringing together artists and creatives to explore the relationship between art, artificial intelligence, emerging technologies, democracy, community and public life.
The fellowship is open to emerging, mid-career and established creatives working across different disciplines. Applicants do not need a university degree or previous experience working with AI.
Selected fellows will receive a $3,000 stipend during Year 1 for their participation in the fellowship’s inquiry, co-design, community engagement and collaborative development process.
The application deadline is September 30, 2026.
About the Citizen AI Arts & Technology Fellowship
The fellowship is designed as a space for creatives from different generations, disciplines and professional backgrounds to examine how artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are shaping communities and public life.
Participants will explore questions around creativity, technology, civic participation, democracy, ethics and community engagement.
The programme is particularly interested in creative practices that bring people together, encourage public dialogue or examine the social and cultural effects of technology.
Who Can Apply?
The fellowship welcomes emerging, mid-career and established creatives from diverse professional and creative backgrounds.
You do not need:
- A university or academic degree
- Previous AI expertise
- To work directly with artificial intelligence
However, applicants should have an active creative practice or sustained engagement in a creative field and an interest in the relationship between creativity, technology, community, democracy and public life.
Creative practices may include:
- Visual art
- Performance
- Public and socially engaged art
- Design
- Digital media
- Filmmaking
- Creative technology
- Music
- Movement
- Fibre and textile arts
- Writing
- Storytelling
- Interdisciplinary practice
Other creative forms may also be considered.
Areas of Interest
The fellowship encourages applications from creatives whose work or interests connect with one or more of the following areas:
- Community-engaged, socially engaged or participatory practice
- Public art and placemaking
- Arts-based research and storytelling
- Public dialogue and facilitation
- Democracy and civic participation
- Belonging and community voice
- Social, cultural and ethical questions around technology
- Critical or experimental approaches to AI
- Technology and society
- Community organising
- Education and advocacy
- Public engagement
Applicants are not expected to agree on the role AI should play in society. The programme welcomes critical, supportive and questioning perspectives on emerging technologies.
What Are the Fellowship Benefits?
$3,000 Year 1 Stipend
Selected fellows will receive a $3,000 stipend in Year 1 for participation in the fellowship’s inquiry, co-design, community engagement and collaborative development process.
Participation in designated Citizen AI workshops or activities outside the core fellowship commitment will be compensated separately.
Year 2 Opportunities
The fellowship is expected to move into a more intensive implementation phase in Year 2.
Selected participants may have opportunities to become more involved in areas such as:
- Production
- Fabrication
- Facilitation
- Public programming
- Implementation of ideas developed during Year 1
Compensation for Year 2 will reflect the scope and level of engagement.
What Are the Requirements?
Applicants should be able to demonstrate:
- An active creative practice or sustained engagement in a creative field
- Interest in creativity, technology, community, democracy and public life
- Experience or demonstrated interest in collaborative, participatory, community-engaged or public-facing work
- Curiosity about artificial intelligence and emerging technologies
- Willingness to consider both the possibilities and challenges of technology
- Commitment to respectful, inclusive and ethical engagement
- Ability to participate consistently in bi-monthly fellowship meetings and collaborative activities
Who Is This Fellowship For?
The fellowship may be relevant to artists, writers, designers, filmmakers, musicians, storytellers, digital creatives, community organisers, educators and other creative practitioners whose work intersects with technology and public life.
You do not have to identify as an AI specialist to apply.
The call is instead looking for people with creative practices and an interest in exploring how technology intersects with communities, democracy and society.
How to Apply
Interested applicants should complete the Citizen AI Arts & Technology Fellowship 2026–2027 application form online.

Applicants should submit their applications before the deadline.

Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa announced the plan at the 2026 Ondo State Entrepreneurs Summit held at The Dome in Akure, where more than 8,000 entrepreneurs gathered to discuss emerging business opportunities.

He urged entrepreneurs to move beyond simply starting businesses and focus on building enterprises capable of surviving changes in markets and technology.
According to the governor, government’s role is not to create dependency but to provide an environment where entrepreneurs can identify and access opportunities that can support sustainable growth.
Aiyedatiwa also encouraged beneficiaries to use the support responsibly, pay their taxes and mentor others, while urging entrepreneurs who were not selected for direct support to apply the knowledge gained at the summit to strengthen their businesses.
The summit, organised by Sumi Smart Francis, Special Adviser to the Governor on Entrepreneurship and Innovation, was held under the theme, “Positioning Entrepreneurs for Emerging Opportunities.”

Call for Applications: CDDRL 2027-28 Pre- & Postdoctoral Fellowships
          
The Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law is pleased to invite applications from pre-doctoral students at the write-up stage and from post-doctoral scholars working in any of the four program areas of democracy, development, evaluating the efficacy of democracy promotion, and rule of law. The application cycle for the 2027-2028 academic year will be open from Monday, September 21, 2026, through Monday, November 30, 2026.
Our goal is to provide an intellectually dynamic environment that fosters lively exchange among Center members and helps everyone to do excellent scholarship. Fellows will spend the academic year at Stanford University focusing on research and data analysis as they work to finalize and publish their dissertation research while connecting with resident faculty and research staff at CDDRL.
Pre-doctoral fellows must be enrolled currently in a doctoral program or equivalent through the time of intended residency at Stanford and must be at the dissertation write-up (post-coursework) phase of their doctoral program. Post-doctoral fellows must have earned their Ph.D. within 3 years of the start of the fellowship, or plan to have successfully defended their Ph.D. dissertations by July 31, 2027.
In addition to our regular call for applications, CDDRL invites applications for the following fellowships:
Gerhard Casper Fellow in Rule of Law: We welcome research on any aspect of rule of law, including judicial politics, criminal justice, and the politicization of judicial institutions. We are an interdisciplinary center; candidates from any relevant field (i.e., the social sciences, law) are welcome to apply. This is a 9-month, residential fellowship, and the Gerhard Casper Fellow will be part of CDDRL’s larger cohort of pre- and postdoctoral fellows. Please apply through the CDDRL fellowship application process and indicate that you would like to be considered for the Gerhard Casper Rule of Law Fellowship.
Jan Koum Israel Studies Program Fellow: We welcome research on any aspect of modern Israel, including Israeli politics, constitutionalism, economics, society, diplomacy, and international affairs. We are an interdisciplinary center; candidates from any relevant field (i.e., the social sciences and law) are welcome to apply. This is a 9-month, residential fellowship, and the Jan Koum Israel Studies Program Fellow will be part of CDDRL’s larger cohort of pre- and postdoctoral fellows. Please apply through the regular CDDRL fellowship application process and indicate that you would like to be considered for the Jan Koum Israel Studies Program Fellowship.
